# Shadow Futures

> Shadow Futures is a book and research project by Martin Erlic about contribution uncertainty in self-reinforcing markets. The book is "Shadow Futures: How Markets Choose Winners—and Lose Sight of the Alternatives." The original paper is "Shadow Futures: Contribution Uncertainty and the Self-Reinforcing Market." A market can reward real productive inputs while exhausting the independent comparisons needed to determine what those inputs contributed to the eventual rewards.

## Primary sources

- [Free book and chapter guide](https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/book): The complete general-audience book, synopsis, chapter summaries, and free PDF.
- [Complete book PDF](https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/book/shadow-futures.pdf): The free reading edition of "How Markets Choose Winners—and Lose Sight of the Alternatives."
- [Paper landing page](https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/paper): Abstract, research metadata, citation, DOI, and downloads.
- [Full paper PDF](https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/paper.pdf): Searchable 22-page manuscript.
- [SSRN record](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6003994): External working-paper record, abstract 6003994.
- [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6003994): DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6003994.
- [Research collection](https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/papers): The original paper and six companion research drafts on institutions, contestability, measurement, counterfactuals, competition policy, and corrective instruments. The drafts state additional models and assumptions.

The book and the paper are distinct works. DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6003994 identifies the original paper; it does not identify the book or the companion drafts.

## Core definitions

- Shadow futures: unrealized positive-probability market histories with the same productive inputs, rules, and initial state but different allocation shocks and terminal rewards.
- Contribution uncertainty: uncertainty about how much observed productive inputs causally contributed to realized rewards after passing through a self-reinforcing allocation process.
- Comparison budget: the cumulative probability that the next allocation could go to someone other than the current favorite.
- Epistemic monopoly: control over the production of the independent comparison paths needed to explain an allocation.

## Book citation

Erlic, Martin. "Shadow Futures: How Markets Choose Winners—and Lose Sight of the Alternatives." Free reading edition, 2026. https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/book.

## Original paper citation

Erlic, Martin. "Shadow Futures: Contribution Uncertainty and the Self-Reinforcing Market." First posted December 2025; revised October 2026. SSRN abstract 6003994. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6003994.
